title: Systemic Integrative Mechanisms and Intervention Strategies in Exercise-Induced Skeletal Muscle Damage: Evidence from Animal, Clinical, and Multi-Omics Studies
abstract: Exercise-induced muscle damage (EIMD) has classically been attributed to localized mechanical disruption following eccentric contractions. Emerging evidence, however, indicates that EIMD represents a systems-level failure of stress integration within skeletal muscle rather than a purely mechanical lesion. Mechanical loading initiates disturbances in intracellular Ca2+ homeostasis, which interact with metabolic stress, redox imbalance, and immune activation to form self-reinforcing feedback loops. When compensatory capacity is exceeded, transient injury may shift toward maladaptive remodeling marked by mitochondrial dysfunction, ferroptosis, chronic inflammation, and impaired regeneration. Recent studies identify reactive oxygen species accumulation, iron-dependent lipid peroxidation, dysregulated energy sensing, and aberrant immune polarization as key molecular tipping points governing injury reversibility. Beyond their regenerative role, satellite cells act as integrators of metabolic history and epigenetic memory, linking repetitive injury to reduced muscle adaptability, age-related sarcopenia, and heightened metabolic disease risk. Here, we synthesize evidence from animal models, clinical studies, and multi-omics analyses to establish a systems biology framework for EIMD. We delineate the spatiotemporal interactions among mechanical, metabolic, oxidative, immune, and regenerative modules; identify regulatory nodes that determine adaptive repair versus pathological outcomes; and critically evaluate current nutritional, physical, pharmacological, and regenerative interventions from a mechanism-oriented perspective. Finally, we discuss how multi-omics, digital monitoring, and individualized rehabilitation may enable precision management of EIMD and advance understanding of muscle stress resilience and adaptive limits.

title: Genome-Wide Identification and Analysis of the WRKY Transcription Factor Family Associated with Leaf Senescence in Alfalfa.
abstract: Leaves are the most significant parts of forage crops such as alfalfa. Senescence is the terminal stage of leaf development and is controlled by an integrated myriad of endogenous signals and environmental stimuli. WRKY transcription factors (TFs) play essential roles in regulating leaf senescence; however, only a few studies on the analysis and identification of the WRKY TF family in Medicago Sativa have been reported. In this study, we identified 198 WRKY family members from the alfalfa ( M. sativa L.) cultivar 'XinjiangDaye' using phylogenetic analysis and categorized them into three subfamilies, Groups I, II, and III, based on their structural characteristics. Group II members were further divided into five subclasses. In addition, several hormone- and stress-related cis-acting elements were identified in the promoter regions of MsWRKYs . Furthermore, 14 aging-related MsWRKYs genes from a previous transcriptome in our laboratory were selected for RT-qPCR validation of their expression patterns, and subsequently cloned for overexpression examination. Finally, MsWRKY5 , MsWRKY66 , MsWRKY92 , and MsWRKY141 were confirmed to cause leaf yellowing in Nicotiana benthaminana using a transient expression system. Our findings lay a groundwork for further studies on the mechanism of M. sativa leaf aging and for the creation of new germplasm resources.

title: Brain endothelial cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway in aging and neurodegeneration
abstract: The cyclic GMP-AMP synthase (cGAS)–stimulator of interferon genes (STING) signaling pathway has emerged as a key mediator of neuroinflammation. While current studies primarily attribute its effects to neurons and glial cells, emerging research suggests that cGAS-STING signaling may play a critical role in cerebral vasculature, particularly in brain endothelial cells. Therefore, studying the role of inflammation caused by the cGAS–STING pathway in brain endothelial cells could provide a more comprehensive understanding of neuroinflammatory disease and new avenues for therapeutic interventions. Here, we review the multifaceted role of global cGAS–STING signaling in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases and the potential contribution of cGAS–STING in brain endothelial cells. The vascular system in the brain creates a unique environment crucial for proper brain functioning (Sweeney et al., 2019). Inflammation in blood vessels compromises both vascular and cerebral function. It is increasingly recognized as a critical factor contributing to the development of various neurological disorders. Recent research has indicated that cGAS–STING signaling, an innate immunity pathway (Paul et al., 2021), may play a central role in vascular inflammation. Neurovascular inflammation in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation is a prevalent feature and plays a pivotal role in aging and neurodegenerative disorders (Paul et al., 2021). While neuroglia are increasingly studied in aging and neurodegeneration, less is known about the contribution of the vasculature and brain endothelial cells (BECs), which represent another significant site of inflammation in the central nervous system (CNS). Neurovascular inflammation results in blood–brain barrier (BBB) leakage, dysfunction of the neurovascular unit, and hypoxia. This amplifies the inflammatory response within the CNS, contributing to neuronal dysfunction and damage (Sweeney et al., 2019). As the primary barrier in blood vessels between blood and the surrounding tissues, the endothelial cells (ECs) are a key player in vascular inflammation. BECs have especially great importance as they—together with pericytes and astrocytes—form the multicellular BBB and contribute to the selective permeability of the BBB (Sweeney et al., 2019). By interacting with both immune signaling molecules in the blood and CNS immune cells, BECs act as an important bridge between functions of the innate immune system, making them an interesting target for anti-inflammatory treatment. Endothelial inflammation is a multifaceted process involving various mechanisms. Recent research has indicated that the cGAS-STING pathway may be involved in triggering the inflammatory processes in endothelial cells (Yu et al., 2022). The aim of this perspective is to examine the potential role of BEC cGAS–STING in various neurological and neuroinflammatory diseases. We first review the role of global cGAS–STING signaling in these diseases. We then discuss the current evidence of the cGAS–STING pathway in triggering endothelial inflammation and dysfunction. The cGas–STING pathway overview: cGAS–STING signaling serves as a crucial regulator of inflammatory responses (Paul et al., 2021). This pathway, designed to sense DNA within the cell and trigger an immune response, acts as a surveillance mechanism for damaged and infected cells. DNA triggering this response can originate from diverse sources. Pathogenic sources include double-stranded DNA viruses, retroviruses, some intracellular bacteria, and parasitic protozoans. Moreover, self-DNA—both extracellular and genomic—and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) can also activate cGAS under specific circumstances (Paul et al., 2021). cGAS recognizes long double-stranded DNA in the cytoplasm and undergoes activation to synthesize 2′,3′-cGAMP (Figure 1). This molecule then binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, leading to STING oligomerization and translocation to the Golgi. In the Golgi, STING recruits TANK-binding kinase 1 (TBK1) to form a signalosome, facilitating TBK1 autophosphorylation. Subsequently, TBK1 phosphorylates STING, providing a docking site for interferon (IFN) regulatory factor 3 (IRF3), which is also phosphorylated by TBK1. Activated IRF3 forms dimers and translocates to the nucleus, stimulating the transcription of type I IFNs and other IFN-stimulated genes. Additionally, the cGAS-STING pathway activates nuclear factor-κB, mitogen-activated protein kinase, and the STING-PERK signalosome within the endoplasmic reticulum, further contributing to the ensuing immune response.Figure 1: Schematic diagram of activation of the cGAS–STING signaling pathway in BECs.During aging and neurogenerative conditions, cytosolic DNA is recognized by cGAS, leading to the synthesis of a 2′,3′-cGAMP. 2′,3′-cGAMP binds to STING in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, causing STING transportation to the proximity of the Golgi, where it recruits TBK-1. TBK1 phosphorylates STING, activating the transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB. Activated IRF3 and NF-κB then travel to the nucleus to promote the transcription of type I IFNs and NF-κB inflammatory genes. Alternatively, the cGAS-STING pathway can be activated independently of the DNA sensing pathway. Excessive and continuous production and release of IFN and other inflammatory cytokines resulting from activation of the cGAS-STING pathway can lead to BEC inflammation and dysfunction. This dysfunction results in BBB leakage, allowing IFN, other inflammatory cytokines, plasma proteins, and blood immune cells to permeate into the brain parenchyma. Ultimately, this contributes to the escalation of the neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative process. Created with BioRender.com. BBB: Blood–brain barrier; BEC: brain endothelial cell; cGAS: cyclic GMP–AMP synthase; dsDNA: double-stranded DNA; EC: endothelial cell; IFN: interferon; IRF3: interferon regulatory factor 3; mtDNA: mitochondrial DNA; NF-κB: nuclear factor kappa B; STING: stimulator of interferon genes; TBK1: TANK-binding kinase 1.While the cGAS–STING pathway plays a prominent role in anti-viral, anti-tumor, and inflammatory responses through driving IFN and cytokine production, cGAS and STING also have various functions outside of immunity. cGAS–STING signaling in aging and neurodegeneration: Neuroinflammation emerges as a significant hallmark in numerous neurological disorders. Given the pivotal role of the cGAS–STING pathway in inflammatory processes, there is a compelling rationale to thoroughly investigate this pathway in the context of neurological disorders (Paul et al., 2021). Notably, the cGAS–STING pathway has been implicated in diverse neurological conditions such as brain injury, aging, and neurodegenerative disorders. In particular, brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are highlighted in the following discussion. Aging is the predominant risk factor for the majority of neurodegenerative diseases, often accompanied by the accumulation of senescent cells and inflammation, commonly referred to as inflammaging (Paul et al., 2021). Senescent cells exhibit significant secretory activity known as the senescence-associated secretory phenotype. The dysregulated activity of cGAS–STING is consistently observed among various types of senescent cells, playing a crucial role in the secretion of several senescence-associated secretory phenotype components. Mechanistically, the cGAS–STING pathway triggers the senescence-associated secretory phenotype secretion through the accumulation of cytoplasmic DNA, which is released into the cytosol from the nucleus and mitochondria in senescent cells (Paul et al., 2021). Research has demonstrated that aging-related inflammation is driven by cGAS–STING activation (Gulen et al., 2023). Notably, inhibiting the cGAS-STING pathway in aged mice has been shown to prevent aging-related inflammation and enhance cognitive and motor performance (Gulen et al., 2023). Upon reflection of these findings, it is possible to speculate that the aberrant signaling of cGAS–STING contributes to age-related dysfunction through its pro-inflammatory properties. AD is the most common neurodegenerative disease. Within AD, the aggregation of amyloid-beta and hyperphosphorylated tau induces cellular stress, resulting in mitochondrial dysfunction and the release of mtDNA, which is subsequently recognized by cGAS (Xie et al., 2023). This process triggers heightened expression of type I IFN, provoking neuroinflammation characterized by astrogliosis and microglial activation. Notably, in AD, the STING–IRF3 pathway seems to predominantly activate microglia, exacerbating neuronal damage (Xie et al., 2023). Consequently, the inhibition or deficiency of cGAS in AD models reduces AD pathology, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment (Xie et al., 2023). In summary, it has been consistently revealed that the cGAS-STING pathway undergoes activation during both brain aging and injury, as well as in the progression of neurodegenerative diseases. Across various studies, the manipulation of this pathway through genetic knockout of associated genes or inhibition via chemical interventions has largely demonstrated a reduction in neuronal injury and an improvement in disease outcomes. These compelling results strongly indicate a primarily adverse impact of the cGAS–STING pathway in these conditions, underscoring its significance as a potential target for therapeutic interventions. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of understanding the potential contribution of each cell type in this context. cGAS–STING signaling in brain endothelial cells: Currently, the cell type-specific role of cGAS–STING signaling in the brain is poorly understood. The cGAS–STING pathway has been shown to be activated predominantly in microglia (Gulen et al., 2023; Xie et al., 2023), but it is also present in astrocytes and neurons. While there is little research on the importance of cGAS–STING activity specifically in BECs in neurodegenerative diseases, its significance has been explored in the context of aging (Yu et al., 2022) and various diseases, such as diabetic retinopathy (Liu et al., 2023), COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022), and cerebral malaria (Pais et al., 2022). The common activators of the cGAS–STING pathway mentioned above, such as viral, bacterial, and self-DNA, have been shown to activate this pathway in BECs. During aging, mitochondrial dysfunction in blood vessels leads to the release of mtDNA into the cytoplasm. Simultaneously, nuclear DNA damage increases the amount of cytoplasmic chromatin fragments. These processes activate the cGAS–STING pathway in endothelial cells, contributing to aging-related endothelial dysfunction. Evidence of the activation of the cGAS-STING pathway is shown by the increased expression of cGAS, STING, and p-IRF3 in older aortic endothelial cells compared with younger ones, both in aged mice and humans (Yu et al., 2022). Consequently, inhibiting cGAS or STING in aging models improves endothelial function, reduces senescence, and decreases the levels of aging markers (Yu et al., 2022). Diabetic retinopathy is a common microvascular complication in diabetes mellitus, characterized by damage to the retinal blood vessels, which can lead to vision impairment or even blindness. cGAS-STING was found to be crucial to retinal endothelial cell senescence, inflammation, and the consequent capillary degeneration (Liu et al., 2023). Interestingly, by measuring free-floating DNA in the diabetic eyes, significantly higher levels of extracellular DNA are observed in diabetic patients compared with nondiabetic controls, suggesting a key role for increased free-floating extracellular DNA in the activation of the cGAS–STING pathway (Liu et al., 2023). In COVID-19, infection with SARS-CoV-2 causes mitochondrial dysfunction and mtDNA release in endothelial cells in the skin, lungs, and brain, which activates cGAS–STING signaling, leading to cell death and type I IFN production. This process is a key driver of the overall inflammatory response, significantly contributing to the pathogenesis of COVID-19 (Domizio et al., 2022). Remarkably, pharmacological inhibition of STING reduces severe lung inflammation induced by SARS-CoV-2 and improves disease outcomes in mice. In further support of the role of BEC cGAS-STING signaling in brain disease, a recent study showed that BECs are the main cell drivers of the STING1-IFN axis in the brain during cerebral malaria, a fatal neurological complication of malaria infection (Pais et al., 2022). The study identified extracellular particles released from Plasmodium (the parasite responsible for malaria)-infected erythrocytes bind STING1 and activate the STING1-dependent type I IFN response in BECs (Pais et al., 2022). Furthermore, it pinpointed heme, a product of hemoglobin degradation within these extracellular particles, as a potential STING1 ligand. In addition, a recent study has shown that cGAS-STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway, for example, by vascular endothelial growth factor (Luo et al., 2023). Vascular endothelial growth factor activates the pathway by stimulating cGAS nuclear translocation via an importin-β pathway. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs results in increased production of type I IFNs and other cytokines (Figure 1). Type I IFNs from BECs, together with those from microglia, astrocytes, and neurons, elicit the interferon response, exacerbating or possibly even initiating neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration. They signal through the heterodimeric receptor (IFNAR) and Janus kinase/signal transducer and activator of transcription signaling cascade, activating IFN signaling and stimulating the transcription of interferon-stimulated genes (Paul et al., 2021). These interferon-stimulated genes include proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-1β, interleukin-6, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha. In addition to their role in natural immunity, interferon-stimulated genes are essential in the pathogenesis of CNS disorders including neuroinflammatory and neurodegenerative diseases (Paul et al., 2021). Type I IFNs produced by other cell types or by the endothelium itself can activate the IFNAR on BECs, i.e., binding to IFNARs on BECs in an autocrine and paracrine fashion. Activation of the IFN signaling pathway in BECs can result in neurovascular inflammation and BBB leakiness through multiple mechanisms: (1) Promoting endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, senescence, or death (Domizio et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023); (2) Impairing BBB integrity by downregulation of adherens junction protein VE-cadherin and tight junction proteins such as occludin and claudin-5 (Jana et al., 2022); (3) Enhancing leukocyte recruitment and infiltration (Pais et al., 2022). These findings prompt us to propose the significance of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs in aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Indeed, elevated STING expression is observed primarily in BECs in various neurodegenerative diseases including AD, PD, ALS, and multiple sclerosis (Ferecsko et al., 2023). Consistent with this, recent single-cell/nucleus RNA sequencing of BECs from aged mice and human AD brains (Yang et al., 2022) has revealed heightened IFN inflammatory responses and IFN expression, hinting a possible role of the cGAS-STING signaling in neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration in the context of aging and AD. We therefore propose that the abnormal activation of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs not only triggers BEC inflammation and dysfunction, but also exacerbates or even initiates a cascade of events culminating in the unrestrained and prolonged synthesis of inflammatory genes. Concurrently, the BBB’s integrity is compromised, marked by increased permeability and leakage. BBB disruption then facilitates the infiltration of harmful peripheral substances into the brain parenchyma, fueling the escalation of neuroinflammation and neurodegeneration (Figure 1). BBB dysfunction is a pathological hallmark shared by both aging and AD and is believed to play a pivotal role in driving downstream neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration, and cognitive decline (Sweeney et al., 2019). However, while appreciation of the pathological significance of BBB dysfunction has been growing, the direct cause-and-effect link between BBB dysfunction and disease progression, as well as the molecular mechanisms underlying BBB dysfunction, is still not fully understood. Activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may offer a potential molecular mechanism in understanding this connection and BBB dysfunction. Conclusions and perspectives: Excessive cGAS–STING activity in microglia, astrocytes, and neurons occupy an important role in the inflammation and pathogenesis of brain aging and neurodegenerative diseases, but BECs also have high cGAS–STING activity under these conditions (Ferecsko et al., 2023). The significance of cGAS–STING activation in peripheral ECs across various diseases prompts us to contemplate the potential importance of cGAS–STING in BECs in the context of aging and neurodegeneration. We hypothesize that aberrant activation of cGAS–STING signaling in BECs may trigger neurovascular inflammation and play a pivotal role in aging and neurodegeneration. Therefore, targeting cGAS–STING activation in BECs may attenuate endothelial dysfunction and brain inflammation, and should be an intriguing avenue for future inquiry regarding brain aging and neurodegeneration. Targeting signaling pathways in BECs offers a potential advantage of bypassing the BBB, a significant challenge in drug development. To date, few studies have examined the role of the cGAS–STING pathway in BECs in neurodegenerative disorders. Therefore, further research using BEC-specific approaches is needed to evaluate this hypothesis. BECs in arterial, capillary, and venous locations exhibit differences in transcriptomes in response to circulatory cues related to aging, innate immunity, and oxidative stress, with more significant changes in capillary BECs (Yang et al., 2022). It would be interesting to investigate whether the location of BECs exhibits differences in the activity and response of the cGAS–STING pathway during disease. As discussed above, cGAS–STING signaling can also be activated in ECs independently of the DNA sensing pathway (Luo et al., 2023). This raises an intriguing question: Can the cGAS–STING pathway be triggered in a DNA-independent manner in the context of neurodegeneration, and what roles do DNA-dependent and DNA-independent mechanisms play in this process? Another area of research is to study the interplay between BECs and the component cells of the brain. Could disruptions in the pathway within the brain cells produce secondary alterations in the endothelium? Answers to these questions will provide significant insights into this innate immune system and have therapeutic implications for treating neurodegenerative diseases. title: Innovative CRISPR-Cas9 Strategies for Epigenetic Modulation of HIV-1 Latency: Targeting Tissue-Specific Reservoirs with Multiplexed Approach
abstract: The most significant barrier to curing HIV-1 is the persistence of HIV-1 in latent reservoirs, distinct populations of long-lived, transcriptionally silent cells located in blood, lymphoid tissues, gastrointestinal (gut-associated lymphoid tissue), and central nervous system, which necessitate lifelong antiretroviral therapy but reliably fail to result in viral eradication. Maintenance of these reservoirs in an epigenetic state is achieved by DNA methylation, a repressive chromatin remodelling and histone modification and is the mechanism that evades immune detection of the integrated proviruses. Several promising advances are noted herein, such as multiplexed guide RNAs to concurrently target multiple proviral and host regulatory sites; tissue-specific delivery through viral vectors with tissue-specific promoters, ligand-decorated lipid nanoparticles, and exosome delivery; and a concept of integrating combinatorial gene editing with latency reversing agents and broadly neutralizing antibodies to increase immune-mediated eradication. Complimentary preclinical verification procedures such as humanized mouse models and skilled organoids exhibit the security, performance, and versatility of such disciplines. A paradigm shift necessitated by the evidence is a global shift to personalized, reversible epigenetic modelling of latency to overcome heterogeneity and anatomical compartmentalization in the reservoir. In future progress in delivery, specificity, and multi-omic profiling is expected to propel faster clinical translation, not only in HIV-1 but also in other chronic viro-infections, and mark the dawn of a new age of curative genomic medicine.

title: Pathology At the Edge of Certainty: Flesh, Code, and the Semiotics of Diagnosis
abstract: Pathology has long been a discipline suspended between visibility and obscurity, an art of extracting intelligibility from the silent mutterings of tissues. To incise, to stain, to digitize, to sequence, these are not merely techniques but ritual gestures through which disorder is rendered interpretable. Yet what pathology produces is never pure truth, but a mediated translation, a provisional rendering of the biological into the semiotic. The cell, the nucleus, the chromatin granule: each appears as an emblem to the eye, but each resists finality, slipping away into interpretive ambiguity the closer one attempts to grasp it. The nineteenth-century pathologist relied upon gross inspection and rudimentary dyes, believing that morphology itself was destiny. The twentieth century elaborated this grammar into histochemistry, electron microscopy, and immunohistochemistry, embedding within our craft the conviction that colorimetric stains and antibodies could stabilize meaning. But the twenty-first century has dissolved such stability. Next-generation sequencing has flooded our discipline with torrents of data, revealing mutational architectures of disease at single-base resolution, while spatial transcriptomics has reintroduced the geography of expression, situating genes not merely as abstractions but as occupants of precise microanatomical niches. Digital pathology has transformed slides into gigapixel matrices, to be parsed not only by human eyes but by convolutional neural networks trained on thousands of diagnostic exemplars. The laboratory is no longer defined by its microscopes alone; it is also a data centre, a hub of algorithms, a crucible in which flesh becomes code. And yet, with every new instrument of precision, pathology discovers its new uncertainties. Sequencing yields variants of unknown significance, exquisite in detail but impoverished in interpretation. Artificial intelligence classifies patterns with uncanny speed, but its inner logics remain opaque, inviting both wonder and distrust. Spatial genomics reveals neighbourhoods of cellular discourse, but the language of these interactions is not yet fully decipherable, resembling more a constellation of whispers than a transcript of intent. The dream of certainty, of a seamless translation from lesion to truth, recedes ever further even as resolution sharpens. The reader will find in this volume not a handbook of protocols, but a meditation on what it means to diagnose in the age of data deluge. The chapters trace how pixels become prognosis, how gigabases of sequence intersect with the delicate geometries of histology, how autopsy in the molecular era acquires an afterlife of interpretation. Here, pathology is no longer only a science of morphology, but an epistemology that straddles histology, bioinformatics, systems biology, and machine learning. It asks: what is a slide when it is also an image dataset? What is a cell when its signature can be reduced to both morphology and transcriptome? What is a prognosis when it emerges not from the intuition of the pathologist alone but from the fusion of human judgment and algorithmic inference? To engage pathology today is to navigate a terrain where biological tissue, digital pixels, and molecular codes interpenetrate. Certainty does not reside in any of these alone; it resides, if at all, in the fragile interpretive act of weaving them together. Pathology at the edge of certainty is therefore pathology as translation, between matter and data, between noise and meaning, between death and its decipherment. And in that act of translation lies not finality, but an unending search, a discipline defined by its humility before complexity and its persistence in rendering the obscure slightly more legible.

title: Could psilocin rescue chronic, stress-accelerated, transcriptional aging in brain?
abstract: Brain aging (BA) processes are complex, often affect multiple systems, and frequently lead to cognitive decline and increased susceptibility to insults. BA appears to be a primary risk for the development of many prominent neurodegenerative pathologies. The US Census Bureau predicts that the aging population (65+) will represent a greater proportion of the US population than children (under 18) by 2034, dramatically increasing the burden on health-care infrastructure.17 Several mechanisms of stress driven, aging-related neurologic dysfunction have been advanced in the past 50 years and include: Stress hormone exposure and glucocorticoid cascade;7, 16 calcium ion dyshomeostasis;8 allostatic load;10 and neuroinflammation.14 Taken together, these data suggest that many aspects of BA are accelerated, or even recapitulated, by stress. Here, the hippocampus (HIP) is an appropriate model structure based on its well-established role in cognition and memory, its manifestation of aging and stress-driven changes in gray (GM) and white matter (WM) transcriptional profiles, and its vulnerability to neurodegeneration; further, the HIP is a major target for stress hormones. It is well-recognized that stress’ influence on the limbic system is long-lasting. This may be due to its subcortical localization, evolutionarily conserved pathways, and potentially novel entrainment mechanism compared to the highly plastic neocortical memory processes ordinarily associated with cognition. Despite years of research clearly establishing a link between stress exposure and BA, no interventions targeting this interaction have been approved. We hypothesize that healthy BA and successful resilience to chronic stress would be indicated by improved hippocampal dependent, cognition, reduced stress-behavior, and reduced inflammatory transcriptional signatures; and not merely the persistence of youthful brain dynamics. Taken together, we refer to this constellation of beneficial responses in the aged and/or stressed subject as adaptive remodeling. Psilocin (PSI), the active metabolite of psilocybin, has agonist or partial agonist activity at serotonin [5-Hydroxtryptamine (5-HT)] receptors, including the G-protein coupled receptor subtypes: 5-HT1A, 5-HT1D, 5-HT2A, and 5-HT2C; functional interactions with central dopaminergic systems have also been demonstrated.12 Despite PSI’s known role in 5-HT and dopaminergic signaling, other agents engaging with these systems do not appear to exert similar effects; moreover, it is not clear to what extent PSI engages other glial and neuronal monoaminergic (e.g., serotonin, dopamine, epinephrine, and norepinephrine) systems. PSI has shown strong benefits in human studies and has twice been designated by the FDA as breakthrough therapy; first in 2018 for treatment resistant depression, and again in 2019 for major depressive disorder. Despite substantial interest in the therapeutic potential of PSI, little is known about the mechanisms through which it exerts its effects. An exhaustive search on the Gene Expression Omnibus revealed a single study using transcriptional profiling in ‘brain’ in conjunction with ‘PSI’ treatment (Donovan et al., 2021; GSE 172074). Our lab analyzed raw RNAseq data from this study and identified genes associated with myelin sheath, synapse, and neuron, among others, to be significantly down regulated (p < 0.001) one week after treatment in pig prefrontal cortex. We propose a multi-level study in balanced groups of young and aged, male and female, Fischer 344 rats to investigate PSI’s effects on stress-accelerated BA. In Aim 1, using an ex-vivo hippocampal slice preparation, we will study the acute effects of PSI treatment on HIP. This model will be used to establish PSI concentration-effect relationships, identify responding HIP cell-types using immunohistochemistry or in situ hybridization, as well as to investigate, using RNA-seq, transcriptional profiles from laser capture microdissected hippocampal GM vs WM. Using this nonbiased approach to look at sub-region-specific profiles, will help establish a more complete account of PSI’s mechanism of action. In this prep, we will also measure PSI’s influence on basic electrophysiology properties like synaptic strength, conduction velocity and after-hyperpolarizing potential. PSI’s chronic effect on HIP-dependent cognitive behavior has also not been fully elucidated in prior studies. We will address this gap in Aim 2 of our study by using the Morris water maze test after 12-week chronic restraint [3hrs/day, 4days/week, using disposable DecapiCone restraint (or 3D printed ‘Restraint Device’ if approved)]. In human trials,1, 3, 5, 15 PSI has been used as an adjunct to guided psychotherapy (PT). To date, there are no recognized animal models of PT; though, enriched environments such as, social interaction, have been shown to be beneficial in animal models of neurodegenerative disease.9 We will attempt to mimic PT in our animal model with enriched group housing vs single housing. Regardless of whether results support our hypothesis, the significance of this project derives from its potential both for elucidating basic mechanisms of interactions between stress and BA, and for suggesting new therapeutic approaches to major health-related problems that widely affect the elderly.
